newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir cosmonauts talk to families on new video link.
newsitem.headline: Mir cosmonauts talk to families on new video link.

text.p: Russian cosmonauts aboard the damaged Mir space station spoke to their families on Sunday in a new two-way video link ahead of one of the toughest weeks in the long history of Moscow's space programme.

Mir has been limping around the Earth with reduced power since a cargo craft collided with the station on June 25, puncturing its Spektr science module and causing a loss of about half of the power from solar panels.

"At 8 p.m. the two Russian cosmonauts, Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, spoke with their families for half an hour in a two-way video link, and the quality of the reception was excellent," a Mission Control spokesman said.

He said this was due to new transmitters sent up as part of a cargo shipment last week. The equipment will also help Russian Space Agency officials on Earth coordinate repairs expected to take place very early on Thursday morning.
British-American NASA astronaut Michael Foale spoke to his wife by radio, he said.

On Monday, Mission Control plans to use the improved video link to beam up images of repair simulations engineers outside Moscow have done wearing space suits in a swimming pool inside a replica of the space station.
The crew will study the 20-minute film before undertaking their own dress rehearsal. The aim is for a cosmonaut to reattach 17 internal cables and restore power from some of Spektr's solar panels.

The accident was the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history and another blow to the prestige of the Russian Space Agency, which took responsibility for the programme after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 and has since come under severe financial pressure.

"Tomorrow the state commission (tackling the crisis) will decide the final date for going into the Spektr module," a duty officer at Mission Control outside Moscow told Reuters on Sunday. "At the moment we think it will take place in the night from July 17 to 18."
The future of Mir depends on the cosmonauts' repairs.
On Tuesday, the crew plan a dress rehearsal lasting up to six hours. The repair job is made more difficult by ther fact that the astronaut has to wear a bulky space suit in Mir's cramped interior.
A second cosmonaut will stand by in reserve nearby, while Foale sits in the Soyuz escape module.

During the repairs a new hatch will be installed separating Spektr from Mir's other cluttered array of modules. Unlike the old hatch, the new one can be closed without requiring the cables to the solar panels to be unplugged.
